Hoult, 36, is best known for his roles in the X-Men franchise, Mad Max: Fury Road, Nosferatu and Superman, playing the evil Lex Luthor in the latter and in the upcoming sequel Man Of Tomorrow.

As for Pattinson, 40, the actor needs little introduction. In 27 regions of the Russian Federation, the immunodeficiency virus is spreading among the entire population, not only risk groups, according to the latest Rospotrebnadzor data. People increasingly pass the virus to one another, often unaware they are infected.

In 27 Russian regions, there is a generalised HIV epidemic. This was reported by the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor. Scientists use this term for the stage when the human immunodeficiency virus spreads in the general population rather than only among risk groups.

In these regions, HIV is diagnosed in more than 1% of pregnant women. The situation is most serious in the Kemerovo, Irkutsk and Sverdlovsk regions.

And although, according to the Central Research Institute for the Prevention and Control of AIDS, 45,000 new HIV cases were detected in Russia in 2025, which is 13.4% lower than in 2024, last year a record was set for the number of HIV and hepatitis infections in medical institutions, according to statistics compiled by the specialist portal Medvestnik.

Experts record the highest level of HIV and hepatitis infections in medical facilities in 15 years

These are the highest figures in the past 15 years. Clusters of viral hepatitis C and mixed HIV plus hepatitis infections predominate, said Yelena Igonina, head of the Department for the Epidemiological Wellbeing of the Population at Rospotrebnadzor. In 2025, eight clusters of infection were recorded in healthcare facilities in Russia, with 104 patients infected.

According to Rospotrebnadzor, investigations continued in 2026 into 11 clusters of infection in the territory of ten regions of Russia, where the spread of HIV and hepatitis in medical organisations is suspected. In Moscow, an investigation is underway into a cluster in which 22 cases of viral hepatitis C have been identified.

One of the largest confirmed clusters in the past two years was the infection of 82 people in a sanatorium in Kabardino-Balkaria. While receiving medical care, 76 patients contracted viral hepatitis C and six were found to have mixed infections. In oncology hospitals in Kamchatka Territory and Buryatia, 147 and 42 patients, respectively, were infected with hepatitis. Another three hepatitis C clusters were identified in dialysis centres in the Samara and Kursk regions, where 26 people were affected.

Experts describe violations of sanitary and epidemiological rules as the main cause of the infections, including the use of single-use catheters or glucometers on several patients. In such situations, the source is usually patients with undiagnosed infections.

Yelena Igonina notes that these "systemic and gross violations" have become entrenched in today’s Russia. Although simultaneous testing for hepatitis C antibodies and RNA covers blood, component, organ and tissue donors well, testing for RNA among other categories that should be tested, namely dialysis, haematology and transplant patients, contacts in hepatitis clusters, children under one born to mothers with HIV and patients with immunodeficiency, is significantly lagging behind.

In addition, for the first time in six years, two cases of HIV infection via transfusion of blood components were identified in 2026, the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor added.

When hospitals receive large numbers of people with undiagnosed infections, international HIV consultant Aleksei Verter told Current Time, this means that "the infectious process in the country is latent, hidden" and a great many people do not know they are infected.

Despite lower mortality, the number of people living with HIV is rising

Despite a decline in HIV incidence and mortality in Russia in recent years, the number of people infected continues to grow, Medvestnik’s authors note. Statistics show that for each death there are one and a half new infections, that is, the number of people "living with HIV continues to grow constantly", explains Natalya Ladnaya.

The decline was preceded by a long period of rising incidence, but in the past three years rates of morbidity and mortality among people with HIV have been falling and, according to her preliminary data, this trend will continue in 2026. At the same time, the expert is convinced that there is no reason to rest on one’s laurels, since "the dynamics can change rapidly".

In recent years, the number of deaths from HIV in Russia has been between 30,000 and 34,000 per year. This is an extremely high figure, stresses the head of the research department for the prevention and control of AIDS at the Central Research Institute of Rospotrebnadzor. "Among all the countries in the world there are only 15 where more than 15,000 deaths of people with HIV are recorded, including Russia." "The highest HIV incidence rates per 100,000 population in the European region are in Russia, Ukraine and North Macedonia", says Central Research Institute of Epidemiology director and Rospotrebnadzor academician Vasily Akimkin.

HIV infection has become the leading cause of death among Russians of working age. Among men aged 40 to 49, more than 3% are affected by the virus, clarifies Natalya Ladnaya, while the average age of those infected in Russia has increased over the past 15 years from 32 to 44. It is also noteworthy that two-thirds of new HIV transmissions occur through heterosexual contact.

More than 1.232 million people with a confirmed HIV diagnosis now live in Russia, which is 0.8% of the country’s population, Akimkin adds. Rospotrebnadzor has warned that if current approaches to prevention and treatment remain unchanged, the number of people living with HIV in Russia could reach 1.47 million by 2030, according to the agency’s mathematical model. Under this scenario, the annual number of new cases will be between 31,000 and 51,000, and the number of deaths included in the model could rise to 51,000 a year, which is linked, among other things, to population ageing.

In the past seven years, the main causes of death among children with HIV have also changed. An increase in mortality in this group of patients was recorded in 2025 in all federal districts except the Central and Ural districts.

According to an analysis by several Russian media outlets, Rospotrebnadzor and the Health Ministry calculate figures differently. Rospotrebnadzor’s data are more complete, as they are based on laboratory notifications of every positive immunoblot. The Health Ministry’s data are based on the number of people who have been registered for regular follow-up care. As a result, the overall gap between the total number of people with a confirmed diagnosis, 1.23 million according to Rospotrebnadzor, and those actually under medical supervision, 846,500 according to the Health Ministry, amounts to 385,555 people.

600,000 infected people

Only half of people living with HIV in Russia had a suppressed viral load by the end of 2025, said Natalya Ladnaya at the conference "Epidemiological Surveillance of HIV Infection", as quoted by Medvestnik. In practice, this means that at least 600,000 people with HIV "continue to play an active part in transmitting the virus", the expert concludes.

Viral load suppression occurred last year in 77.9% of people with HIV who were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), and "so far it has not been possible to exceed this level", she says, while WHO standards for keeping the epidemic under control are 95-95-95, that is, 95% of people with HIV know their status, 95% of them receive ART and 95% of those on therapy achieve suppression of HIV replication.

As for access to medical care for people living with HIV in Russia, 72% of those infected were under follow-up last year. Despite extensive HIV testing, which has increased by 75% over the past decade and reached 54 million tests last year, effectiveness is declining. In the view of the director of the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor, approaches need to be adjusted by increasing the share of people at the highest risk of infection, who are insufficiently covered by testing. Their share has now almost halved, from 5.8% in 2014 to 3% in 2023.

But the effectiveness of the work is declining, meaning there are more tests, but testing is increasingly carried out among people with a lower probability of having HIV.

Chronic underfunding by the state

The fact that the burden of HIV infection is not decreasing even as incidence falls is reflected in healthcare spending, stresses Natalya Ladnaya. In 2025, spending related to HIV infection was estimated at 279 billion roubles.

In the expert’s view, there is no reason to expect the situation to change; on the contrary, the spread of the virus may intensify among traditionally vulnerable population groups and among people living in regions bordering Ukraine that are characterised by high levels of migration. According to Rospotrebnadzor, incidence and mortality may also rise in the Far Eastern, Southern and North Caucasian federal districts.

Bloggers have also spoken about the spread of viruses, including HIV, among those fighting against Ukraine. According to Anastasia Kashevarova, the Russian authorities should "seriously think about it, there is a threat of an epidemic of socially dangerous diseases", since hepatitis, HIV and tuberculosis are currently spreading in the army and to frontline regions, but "will then spread further into the interior of Russia".

The Insider previously reported that after Russia’s occupation of parts of Donetsk and Luhansk regions, patients with HIV faced shortages of life-saving medicines. The Russian Health Ministry did not include them in centralised drug procurement, and some patients were given medicines past their expiry date.

According to observers, the fact that the healthcare budget is shrinking and all funds are going to the war helps explain, among other things, shortages of sterile consumables in state hospitals.

Other Russian media emphasise that most donors financing HIV prevention programmes for the general population and vulnerable groups have left Russia. The country itself does not adequately fund these projects, says Evgeny Pisemsky, editor-in-chief of the queer media outlet "Parni+", quoted by Current Time. With 45,000 new HIV cases detected in 2025, the draft Russian budget for 2027 provides for additional funding for medicines for only 30,000 new carriers of the virus.

The negotiations will unfold over two days: 10 and 11 November.

"Freedom of navigation in the Black Sea must be restored and preserved. I reiterated my support for his (Zelenskyy's) call for a ceasefire covering food and energy infrastructure."

A spokesperson for the European Council also confirmed the participation.

The institutions will be joined by the E3: France, Germany and the United Kingdom.

The EU team will be led by Bjoern Seibert, von der Leyen's chief of cabinet, and Anna-Maria Boura, chief foreign policy advisor to European Council President António Costa.

Both institutions previously indicated their willingness to engage directly with the Russian delegation, something that has never happened in the context of the peace talks.

At this stage, however, it is not clear if this face-to-face will happen.

Jared Kushner, the US special envoy, said last week that the multilateral format would be organised "if progress is made", though he did not say whether this would be in Abu Dhabi or elsewhere at a later date.

Kushner's long social media post laying down principles to reframe Europe's security architecture after the war has triggered pushback among allies, with Zelenskyy calling it "dangerous". European officials believe the discussion is premature and misguided given that Russia is yet to make a single concession at the negotiating table.

The confirmation of the EU team comes after Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni sent a scathing letter to Costa complaining about the "disarray" in diplomatic formats and demanding the appointment of a special European envoy.

In his reply, Costa agreed to put the issue on the table at this week's informal summit in Dublin, Ireland, which will take place right after the Abu Dhabi meeting.

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski agreed with Meloni and warned that Eastern European's interests should be considered.

"The last thing we want is Western Europe dealing with Russia, over the heads of the East Europeans," Sikorski said from Warsaw.

The Abu Dhabi talks will mark the resumption of trilateral peace negotiations since February, when the war on Iran abruptly shifted Washington's focus.

The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of the Foreign Intelligence Service, together with Kyrylo Budanov and Sergiy Kyslytsya, head and deputy head of the president's office; and Davyd Arakhamia, leader of the ruling party in the Parliament.

The Russian delegation will be headed by Vladimir Medinsky, aide to President Vladimir Putin, and Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin.

The US will be represented by special envoys Steve Witkoff and Kushner.

Trump expressed confidence that an agreement was within reach, although Kyiv and Moscow remain deeply divided over territorial concessions and the security arrangements that would follow any ceasefire.

"There's a very important meeting taking place," Trump said. "I believe that that war is going to end and it's going to end soon. And the only reason it's going to end is because of me."

The US president did not elaborate on what he meant by Ukraine having a different shape or specify which territorial changes he envisaged.

Rubio points to progress on security guarantees

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday that progress had been made in discussions over post-war security arrangements for Ukraine and Europe, suggesting that further advances could follow this week's negotiations.

Speaking ahead of a visit to Paris for talks with G7 foreign ministers, Rubio said a central question was what security arrangements would be needed to protect Ukraine and the wider European continent after the war.

"What is the postwar security infrastructure of Ukraine and more broadly of the European continent going to look like?" Rubio told reporters.

"I think that's what the president's alluding to - is that there's been some advances made in what that architecture could look like post-conflict," he added.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen confirmed that the EU would also be present in Abu Dhabi alongside its partners.

France will also be represented at the negotiations, according to Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot.

Territorial disputes remain a major obstacle

Russia and Ukraine remain far apart over the terms of a potential settlement, particularly the future of Ukrainian territories occupied by Moscow's forces.

Vladimir Putin has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine withdraw its troops from four regions that Moscow illegally claimed to annex in 2022, despite never establishing full control over them.

The Kremlin also insisted that Kyiv abandon its ambitions to join NATO and accept restrictions on the size and capabilities of its armed forces.

Ukraine categorically rejected the demands to cede territory, including areas Russia has failed to capture militarily, and insists that credible security guarantees are essential to prevent another Russian invasion.

Kyiv called for an immediate ceasefire as a first step towards a broader settlement, maintaining that territorial questions would ultimately require direct talks between Zelenskyy and Putin.

Asked about the biggest obstacle to reaching an agreement, Trump pointed to the relationship between the two leaders.

"It was the hatred between Zelensky and Putin," he said.

When asked whether Zelenskyy's hostility towards Putin was understandable given Russia's invasion, Trump referred to what he described as disrespect towards Moscow during an earlier meeting between the two presidents.

Asked whether he trusted Putin or Zelenskyy more, Trump declined to choose.

"I'd rather not say, but I get along with both," he said, adding that he did not believe Putin was deliberately prolonging negotiations.

A physicist has distilled time travel into three lines of proof that shows if spacetime can be sliced into layers of light, every traveller must cross them in the same direction, so no journey can ever loop backwards.

A question many of us have posed in our minds is where would you go if you had a time machine?

Would you head for the year 3000 to see what has become of the human race? Or would you crank the dial backwards like Marty McFly and risk sabotaging your own future? Before you start packing, a physicist has some news that may ruin a few Marvel movies: you may only be able to go one way, and it isn't backwards.

Hongsheng Zhang, a researcher at the University of Jinan in China, has shown that in a broad class of theoretical universes, travelling into your own past is impossible.

The whole argument rests on one fact: "light can never point sideways to a traveller's direction in time," Zhang says.

Imagine spacetime sliced into layers that light itself can travel along. Anything moving slower than light must cross these surfaces in the same direction, like climbing a staircase that never lets you step down.

If you can only ever go up, you can never arrive back on the step where you started.

"My paper asks a narrower question: when does a spacetime permit such a loop, and when does the geometry itself forbid one?" Zhang told Euronews Next.

The two loopholes

Physicists call journeys to the past "closed timelike curves": routes through spacetime that loop back to the very place and moment they began.

"Suppose you wanted to shake hands with your younger self," Zhang says. "To do that you would need a path through spacetime that loops back on itself without ever exceeding the speed of light."

Einstein's equations allow such paths in a handful of scenarios, such as near the core of a spinning black hole.

Crucially, Zhang's research, which has been submitted for peer review, also reveals exactly how a time machine could get around it, and there are only two ways.

The first is twist. Imagine light rays that, instead of travelling side by side, spiral around one another like the strands of a rope. When that happens, the neat surfaces of light can't form, so there is no staircase to keep you climbing.

This is what happens near the centre of a spinning black hole. Einstein's theory says a spinning mass drags space and time around with it, and close to the black hole's core the drag is so strong that moving "forward in time" is bent into a circle.

A traveller following that circle would see their clock ticking forward in time as normal, yet their journey would arrive back at the moment they set off. Physicist Brandon Carter showed in 1968 that such loops exist inside spinning black holes.

But Zhang stresses that twist alone is not the culprit. "Twist on its own does not create a closed curve. It only blocks my argument," Zhang says. "Twist is everywhere in the universe and, as far as we know, harmless."

The second is the shape of the universe itself. The staircase might be perfectly built, but it could lead around the sides of a building, so the top step leads straight back to the bottom, like the impossible staircases in an Escher drawing. You would keep climbing and still end up where you began. Most of the time machines physicists have designed on paper, including those built from wormholes, rely on this trick.

Physicists call this loophole topology, and Zhang believes it is the one to watch. "The loophole that could matter is topology, and that is exactly the one that looks least likely to arise without deliberate engineering," Zhang says.

Destination: tomorrow

Trips to the future, by contrast, are already well established. Einstein showed that moving very fast, or sitting in strong gravity, slows your clock relative to everyone else's. Astronauts returning from six months aboard the International Space Station are about five thousandths of a second younger than they would otherwise have been, according to the European Space Agency.

Zhang is keen to stress the limits of the work. "This is not a claim that time travel is impossible," Zhang says.

For now, though, you may want to pack for tomorrow rather than yesterday... unless you have the Time Stone, of course.

The Coast Guard rescued 18 foreign nationals from the vessel. During the operation, officers also located and recovered twelve bodies from the boat.

Two more incidents involving migrants

At the same time, two other rescue operations were carried out in the wider sea area south of Crete, under the coordination of the JRCC and with the assistance of the European Border and Frontex.

Specifically, a Frontex unmanned aircraft located a second boat carrying about 40 foreign nationals, at a distance of 31 nautical miles southeast of Crete. They were picked up by a vessel of the European force and are expected to be taken to the port of Kaloi Limenes in Crete.

A similar operation followed for a third boat, which was spotted by a Frontex aircraft about 30 nautical miles south of Kaloi Limenes. Some 47 foreign nationals were on board, who were rescued by a ship of the European force and are also expected to be brought to the southern town of Crete.

The tug "Pyrrhos" was immediately mobilised, located the vessel and took on board 28 Sudanese nationals, as well as the body of a man.

Exhibitions

Bruxelles 1900

When: 10 November 2026 - 25 April 2027

Where: Petit Palais (Paris, France)

In around 1893, architect Victor Horta built the Hôtel Tassel (Tassel House) — a masterpiece of design that marked the foundation of Art Nouveau. It's an aesthetic that quickly spread all across Europe, but its first flourishes in Brussels are a key focus of the Petit Palais' new Bruxelles 1900 exhibition. Featuring over 250 works on display, it also highlights Art Deco, comics, illustration and photography; all of the artistic mediums and movements that defined the city's vibrant and influential turn-of-the-20th-century art scene.

Beyond the Streets

When: 11 November 2026 - 5 May 2027

Where: Saatchi Gallery (London, UK)

As far back as ancient Egypt, versions of street art have always existed. The medium as we know it today of urban graffiti, however, took off in '60s and '70s New York and Philadelphia, while artists like Gérard Złotykamień contributed to its rise across Europe. The Saatchi Gallery is digging into this storied history with one of the biggest and most diverse exhibitions on international street culture, bringing together over 100 creators and spanning six decades. Highlights include a large-scale recreation of a graffitied New York subway carriage, a spray paint infinity room and various hip-hop ephemera. Find out more here.

With pensioners worried about cuts and young people unsure they will ever get a pension, company-funded individual schemes have long hovered over Spanish politics. Ahead of the 29N elections, we examine the situation.

The so called Austrian backpack was created in Austria to replace traditional redundancy pay and build up a safety pot. Analysts disagree on whether it would work in Spain. With just a few weeks to go before the general election on 29 November, pensions are once again at the centre of the campaign.

Spain spends around 14,498 million euros a month on contributory Social Security pensions, according to the latest official data for September 2026, an increase of 6.3% on the previous year.

The more than nine and a half million pensioners are closely following the parties' proposals and every mention that might suggest a freeze or cut in these benefits. With an average pension of 1,380 euros (source in Spanish), retirees are watching closely what their future will be in the next legislature, something politicians know very well and use to win the votes of one of the most decisive parts of the population.

Spain's public debt is close to 100% of GDP, more precisely it stood at 99.7%, according to data from August 2026. In other words, 1.75 trillion.

In a country with a population already close to 50 million, an unemployment rate above 10%, where 22.8 million people are in work, earning on average 29,540 euros gross a year, (source in Spanish) workers, and especially young people, wonder whether they will ever receive the benefit they are paying into and whether the system will be able to hold up. In that climate an old economic idea has resurfaced: the Austrian backpack.

A campaign with pensions at its core

Political parties know the immense power of the pensioners' vote and have launched a battle to win those millions of votes that could prove decisive in a set of highly polarised and highly tense elections.

The debate on the sustainability of the system has heated up in recent weeks. The spokesperson for the Partido Popular (PP) in Congress, Ester Muñoz, questioned the viability of the public system, and the Socialist Party (PSOE) and Sumar responded by accusing the PP of wanting to privatise it. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has warned of the "sacrifices" that the leader of the opposition, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, would ask of the population if he were to become the next Spanish prime minister.

The PP leader, however, has promised that if he reaches La Moncloa he will uprate pensions in line with inflation and that "in no case" will he question the public system for these benefits. He has also pledged to "guarantee" the future of pension payments for young people.

The Partido Popular says it believes in a public system and maintains that the only party that has frozen pensions was precisely the PSOE during the Zapatero government.

The clash reflects how sensitive the issue is and the concerns of three groups:

On the one hand, there are the pensioners who fear that their benefits will be frozen or lose purchasing power. On the other side are workers, who see part of their wages cut and paid into a common pot, and wonder whether it will really provide them with a benefit once they retire, doubting that the system will return what they have paid in. Finally, there are the young people who enter a precarious labour market late, with low wages, and expect to retire ever later, with no certainty of receiving a pension.

What is the Austrian backpack?

Its official name is "abfertigung neu" and it works as follows:

Companies pay 1.53% of the worker's gross monthly salary into an individual account, a severance fund. That capital belongs to the employee. The fund tops up the public retirement pension, although it can also be drawn in the event of unemployment or if the worker decides to start a business or become self employed. If the worker dies, the fund is not lost.

In fact, this kind of system is not unique to Austria, Italy has the TFR, which is funded by contributions of 7% of salary. The money follows the worker even if they change employer, which is where the name "backpack" comes from.

This system was introduced in Austria in 2003 to replace traditional redundancy compensation. It is not just a pension fund. In fact, the Austrian backpack does not replace the public pension, as Austria maintains a pay as you go public system, like Spain. The fund was designed as severance pay, and the worker can leave it in their account until retirement in order to supplement their public pension. It is a way of guaranteeing some extra money once they stop working.

Its returns are modest. An Austrian MP from NEOS has said that on average the funds yield around 2%. Austria has approved that, from 2028, workers will be able to choose a model without a capital guarantee and with more equities so they can get more out of their money by taking on risk, or transfer the fund to a pension fund to receive a supplementary income.

What its supporters argue in favour of introducing the Austrian backpack in Spain

Economists from Fedea, José Ignacio Conde Ruiz, Florentino Felgueroso and José Ignacio García Pérez, analysed in 2011 (source in Spanish) how it might be introduced in Spain. Supporters highlight that its portability would make it easier to change jobs without losing rights and that it would create individual savings, a safety net for the worker.

The Bank of Spain defended the idea for years. Pablo Hernández de Cos, governor of the Bank of Spain until 2024, presented it as a possible solution to the long term funding problems of the pension system. In 2023, the bank proposed introducing it using 8,000 million euros of European funds.

Specifically, its proposal was to create a fund in the worker's name into which the company would advance part of the redundancy pay, and that this money could be carried from one job to another in the event of a change. In this way, the employee would receive the accumulated money either when they become unemployed or on retirement.

With this, the Bank of Spain aimed to combat job insecurity and temporary contracts in the labour market, benefit people who change jobs and generate that top up when they reach retirement.

What its critics say: the trade unions, its main opponents

Trade unions such as CC.OO. and UGT argue that it would make dismissal "predictable and financially neutral" for employers, a form of prepaid free dismissal. UGT argues that "it punishes companies that do not dismiss staff, as they have to pay funds into their workforce's accounts month after month, increasing their labour costs, and rewards those that resort more frequently to dismissals, by reducing their cost and ease of financing". They also maintain that this measure "would lead to an increase in the number of dismissals" and in staff turnover, by removing any deterrent effect from compensation.

There are also sceptical voices among expert economists, who point out that it would be difficult to apply because Social Security cannot do without contributions when it faces a structural deficit.

Employers themselves are not enthusiastic about the measure either, fearing that it would increase labour costs.

KPMG has calculated that with the Austrian rate of 1.53% it would not be more beneficial than the current redundancy pay, and that contributions of more than 5.48% would be needed in the case of fair dismissal and more than 9.04% in the case of unfair dismissal.

The key lies in the differences between Spain and Austria. In the event of dismissal, changing employer or becoming self employed in the latter country, the backpack follows the worker, which means it replaces traditional redundancy compensation.

What the parties say

The PP is looking at including the Austrian backpack model once again in its election programme for the 29 November election, as it did in 2023, and maintains that it would not reform the pension system. PSOE and Sumar have repeatedly warned that the PP intends to privatise the system, something the PP denies.

The economic team of José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero tried to introduce the Austrian backpack concept, but it ultimately did not go ahead. Years later, the PSOE tried to develop something similar with publicly promoted occupational pension funds under José Luis Escrivá at the Social Security ministry. A Democratic ‘blue tsunami’ sparked one of the year’s sharpest rotations in Europe: banks rallied, chips sank on data-centre fears.

When Americans voted last week, European investors were watching one question above all: how much room would Donald Trump have left to govern?

By Wednesday morning, they had their answer.

Democrats took control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, a clear defeat for the US president halfway through his term.

On trading floors, the result quickly earned a name: the "blue tsunami".

At first glance, Europe's stock market barely reacted. The Stoxx 600 jumped 1.8% on Wednesday, then gave most of it back. By Friday's close it stood just 0.4% above Tuesday's level.

The Euro Stoxx 50, which tracks the euro area's 50 largest companies, followed the same path. It rose 2% on Wednesday and ended the week just 0.4% higher.

Look beneath the surface, though, and it was one of the most violent reshuffles of the year.

Banks up, tech down

The rotation was clearest at sector level.

European banks rose 3.2% between Tuesday and Friday, with most of the gain on Wednesday alone. Jordi Visser, head of AI macro research at 22V Research, said it was the sector's best week since June.

Travel and leisure stocks did even better, climbing 3.9% as oil prices fell. Brent crude dropped more than 9% on Wednesday, as traders bet that a weakened president would be less likely to escalate the war with Iran.

Utilities gained 2.5% and healthcare 2%. On the other side, energy stocks fell 4.2% on cheaper oil, and technology lost 3.6%.

Europe held up better than Wall Street for a simple reason: its market owns far fewer AI stocks and far more banks.

"The equity market is a distorted mirror of the economy," Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, said in a report.

According to Bell, financial companies make up more than 30% of Stoxx 600 earnings, but only 10% of euro area economic activity. After the midterm tech sell-off, European stocks have now pulled ahead of US equities this year in local-currency terms, according to Goldman Sachs.

"European indices are less exposed to the semiconductor correction," Intesa Sanpaolo's equity strategy team said in a report on Friday. The team added that banks were recovering thanks to solid quarterly results.

Thursday's tech blow-up

Most of the damage in tech came in a single session.

The trigger for Thursday's sell-off was not Congress. It was what happened in the states.

Democrats won governors' races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia. In all three states, Republican governors had courted the data-centre boom with tax breaks and fast-track permits. The upset in Texas, home to some of the largest AI data-centre projects in the US, hit hardest.

At the same time, voters in parts of Ohio, Illinois, Maine and Florida approved local measures to ban or restrict new data centres.

"The fear of Democrat-inspired opposition to data centres has gained greater political weight, and the risk concerns not only new regulations but above all permits, energy consumption and local resistance," Gian Marco Salcioli, head of global markets strategy at Intesa Sanpaolo, said in the report.

If new governors slow approvals, fewer data centres get built. That means fewer chips, fewer machines to make those chips and less equipment to power them.

European technology stocks fell 3.2% on Thursday alone.

Why bond yields fell

Bonds rallied across the board.

Germany's 10-year Bund yield fell from 3.33% on Tuesday to 3.25% on Friday, after touching its lowest level since late August. France's 10-year yield fell further, from 4.95% to 4.77%. The US 10-year Treasury yield dropped from 4.97% to 4.86%.

According to Peter Williams, economist at 22V Research, bond markets see "greater-than-expected constraints on the war, tariffs, and the artificial intelligence (AI) boom as modestly disinflationary shifts over the medium term."

"The market continues to finance the investment programmes of the big hyperscalers, but demands increasingly higher compensation," Intesa Sanpaolo credit strategist Pasquale Lodato said.

A pause in data centres would flip that. Less AI spending would mean less Big Tech debt, and less competition for governments funding their deficits.

Get up to speed on the UN COP31 climate talks kicking off on 9 November, from electrification to emissions.

The UN COP31 climate summit kicks off today in Antalya, Türkiye, as the world treads dangerously close to irreversible damage.

Dozens of leaders from across Europe and further afield will attend two weeks of crucial climate talks. All will arrive with their own agenda and priorities.

They will debate the topics impacting global temperature rise: how countries produce and consume energy, how emissions cuts can get back on track, and how much funding they will give to those who have contributed least to emissions but are being hit hardest, to name just a few.

The conference will run from 9-20 November, culminating in a consensus-based package of decisions on climate action, coupled with a parallel agenda of voluntary actions.

Here’s what you need to know about who’s running this year’s talks, and what’s expected both inside and outside the negotiating room.

Who’s running COP31?

While Türkiye holds the COP31 presidency and will host the COP31 summit, the marathon negotiations will be steered by Australia in an unprecedented arrangement reached after both nations bid to host.

The presidency decides the action agenda – a mechanism for voluntary commitments made outside the formal negotiations, involving companies, cities, banks, investors, civil society, universities and others.

The UN body behind COP talks, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), oversees the negotiating agenda – a different mechanism from the action agenda.

The negotiating agenda sets out what governments will debate and, where appropriate, decide on at COP31. Countries negotiate what’s on the agenda before it is formally agreed – by consensus – and adopted.

Last-minute negotiations over wording are common, with oil and gas producing countries having previously leveraged the consensus-based system to weaken commitments on transitioning away from polluting fossil fuels.

This has led to increasingly loud calls for a new majority vote system – particularly in light of the dangerously slow progress being made towards climate targets.

What’s being debated at COP31?

Electrification and the ‘35-by-35’ target

Electrification is likely to dominate the talks, with Türkiye asking countries to commit to a ‘35-by-35’ target, raising the global share of energy demand by electricity to 35 per cent, up from around 20 per cent, by 2035. We looked at the plan, and why experts aren’t convinced here.

Electrification entails replacing devices, systems or processes that rely on fossil fuels or other non-electric energy with those powered by electricity.

In a recent report, Climate Action Tracker (CAT) found that governments need to electrify much faster if they are to meet the 35-by-35 target – four times faster, in fact.

“Current policies deliver only 28 per cent by 2035, on a trajectory the IEA associates with around 2.5°C of warming by 2100,” the report says.

TAFF: The transition away from fossil fuels

Experts point out, however, that electrification is only as clean as the energy that powers it.

“Taken alone, countries could meet the [35-by-35] target by simply adding electricity to the system (e.g. data centres) or by keeping or even adding fossil fuels to electricity systems,” warns Samuel Guéret, a CAT climate and energy policy analyst with partner organisation Climate Analytics.

“Electrification only limits overshoot if the electricity is cleanly generated, which is why this target should be seen as part of a package with the renewables and efficiency targets agreed at COP28.”

The transition away from fossil fuels – or TAFF – is already a flashpoint in discussions surrounding the summit. But it will not feature on the formal negotiated agenda at COP31.

COP28 in Dubai three years ago saw countries pledge to transition away from fossil fuels for the first time. Since then, progress has stalled, with fossil fuels not even gaining a mention in the final text of COP30. Still, host country Brazil recently published a voluntary global roadmap for the transition, before handing leadership over to Türkiye.

Türkiye, where coal was the largest source of power last year, remains adamant that fossil fuels are required for energy security, with Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar advocating for a “just transition period” to shield those who work in coal mining, while also raising concerns over financing the transition.

Still, this year’s energy crisis prompted by the Iran war has pushed many oil and gas importing countries to ramp up homegrown renewables in the name of security.

The International Energy Agency’s (IEA) recent ‘Renewables 2026’ report forecasts stronger growth in renewables across a wider range of countries in the coming years as governments seek to reduce their exposure to imported fuels and volatile prices.

The EU, which has set a target of cutting emissions by 90 per cent by 2040, has also argued that moving away from fossil fuels is a matter of energy security. It is pushing for faster delivery of existing pledges, including tripling renewables and doubling energy efficiency by 2030.

In Europe, Germany, France and the Netherlands have already established their own roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels. Experts have criticised Germany's 2045 target as being too unambitious, adding that financing of overseas fossil fuel projects is not included in the phaseout.

Methane reduction and the Global Methane Pledge

COP31 will kick off progress on the second Global Stocktake (GST2), a two-year evaluation of progress towards goals laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement, including the commitment to keep global temperature rise well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and ideally within 1.5°C.

The UN warned in September that the world is already set to overshoot the 1.5°C limit, as countries falter on their pledges to curb planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

“We will not look away, and we will not lower our ambition. The 1.5-degree target remains our compass, and our duty is to do everything in our power to return to it,” said Türkiye’s Environment Minister Murat Kurum and COP31 President-Designate, Murat Kurum, ahead of the summit.

While cleaner energy is one way to tackle this, targeting methane emissions has been hailed as an achievable win in the near term.

Although methane stays in the atmosphere for a far shorter time than CO2 before breaking down – around 10-to-12 years versus centuries – it is roughly 80 times more powerful at trapping heat in the atmosphere over a 20-year timeframe. This means even small cuts have an outsized impact on near-term temperature rise.

At COP26 in 2021, over 150 countries joined the voluntary Global Methane Pledge (GMP) to collectively reduce human-caused methane emissions by at least 30 per cent below 2020 levels by 2030, which could prevent over 0.2°C of global warming by 2050.

Methane can be tackled on a number of fronts, from reducing leaks and flaring in oil and gas operations, to improving livestock management and feed efficiency in agriculture, to managing methane emissions from landfills and wastewater.

The EU recently moved to delay a regulation requiring fossil fuel imports to meet the same standards as member states on detecting and repairing methane leaks. It said the move would help to protect energy security and ease market pressures in the oil and gas sectors.

Yet it will co-host a ministerial meeting on the Global Methane Pledge at COP31, where governments will negotiate and coordinate on the initiative. Türkiye has organised a separate Action Agenda on zero waste and methane reduction, focusing on waste-sector emissions.

In October, the US Environmental Protection Agency rolled back 2024 safeguards that limited methane pollution from the oil and gas sector.

While members of Congress and US businesses will attend COP31, there will be no official delegation from the country, which is the world’s second-biggest emitter of greenhouse gases behind China. This is because Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement and has initiated a withdrawal from the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).

Climate finance: Who pays when disaster strikes?

Money is expected to be one of the most contested issues in Antalya, particularly to fund adaptation and loss and damage in countries most vulnerable to climate disasters, like developing nations and small island states.

At COP29 in Baku in 2024, developed countries agreed to mobilise at least $300 billion (€268bn) a year for developing nations by 2035, as part of a wider $1.3 trillion (€1.63tn) target from public and private sources.

At COP30 last year, governments agreed to push for at least a tripling of adaptation finance by 2035, but without settling the baseline, who pays or how the money will be delivered.

A UN Environment Programme (UNEP) report published days before the summit found even tripling current international public adaptation finance would meet just 23-29 per cent of developing countries’ needs.

Where that shortfall comes from and how it is channelled to those who need it is expected to be central to talks at COP31.

Outside the talks: Will protest be allowed at COP31?

For Turkish NGOs, COP31 could offer a rare chance to be heard in a country where, activists say, space for public protest has been steadily shrinking.

A People’s Climate Summit, a grassroots initiative of more than 100 organisations and individuals, will run alongside the talks from 9 November. Organiser Cigdem Ozbas told news agency AFP that more than 1,000 people and 300 organisations from 100 countries have signed up.

The first week will focus on making their demands visible, with forums and evening monitoring sessions in the second week examining proposals they see as greenwashing. A major rally is planned for 14 November, with unions and rights groups expected to join.

Activists are optimistic that COP, as a civil society gathering, won’t face similar crackdowns to July’s NATO summit in Ankara, where police detained more than 4,400 people on terror-related charges, including journalists, civil society leaders and over a dozen environmental volunteers.

But the episode showed how quickly space can be restricted, and Ozlem Katisoz of Climate Action Network Türkiye warned that detentions can happen at any time.

Turkish groups also want a say inside the process. Climate Network Türkiye, a coalition of 15 organisations, is seeking access to negotiators, but there is no formal consultation process. Katisoz has urged visiting delegates to check the presidency’s statements against reality at home, such as the new coal plants still under development.

While there are plenty of affordable options for a ski trip in Europe, there are equally as many if you’re keen to splash some cash.

At the foot of the Matterhorn, the car-free villages provide access to one of the highest ski areas in the entire Alps and almost guaranteed snow – as well as some of the most high-end hotels in the country.

With a total vast slope length of 200 kilometres, daily lift passes cost €111.28 in high season, and accommodation costs €244 per person per night. If you still want to visit on a relative budget, going in low season is a better bet.

Netflix’s EMEA revenue grew 11% year on year in Q3 2026, but sustaining that growth will depend on preserving creative freedom across Europe.

Around 12 years ago, Netflix had no original productions in Europe, and audiences were largely watching content made in, by and for the US.

But it soon became clear that European content couldn't be produced from Los Angeles alone. In 2019, Larry Tanz, Head of Content for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, moved across the pond to Amsterdam to lead the company's European operations. Today, Netflix has 10 regional teams shaping the content audiences watch across Europe.

Over the past decade, Netflix has invested more than €13bn in Europe and, last year, committed to investing a further €1bn in Spain alone by 2028.

Larry joins Hannah Brown in the studio for the first episode of the new series of The Big Question to discuss the secrets behind producing internationally successful content.

‘If you don't make it for someone, you'll end up making it for no one’

Larry has amassed a team of experts across the continent who have an in-depth understanding of their local audiences and creative talent.

“Also they're plugged into what's happening in society, if you develop a film script right now, that film is not going to come out for maybe two years so you can't just try to play on trends of the moment,” Larry told The Big Question.

What might surprise you is that Netflix doesn't approach commissioning projects with the aim of creating a gigantic international hit. Instead, it focuses on producing authentic content that appeals to a specific audience.

“Let’s say you try to make a film in Spain and you cast it with people from everywhere and you try to make it for everybody - you end up making it for nobody and nobody watches it,” Larry explained.

He attributes the success of Squid Game, Netflix’s biggest international hit, to its distinctly Korean style, arguing that its commitment to being unapologetically Korean was precisely what resonated with audiences worldwide.

He emphasised that every Netflix show that has achieved global success has first found an audience in its home market.

Netflix is also one of the few global platforms that dubs and subtitles content in more than 40 languages, making international productions more accessible to audiences worldwide.

And Larry's experience leading Netflix's European operations suggests that this approach is paying off.

A decade ago, non-English-language content accounted for less than 10% of total viewing. Today, that figure has grown to more than a third.

‘Creativity and regulation are not happy bedfellows’

While many of us grew up watching public broadcasters with a clear mandate for their content – the BBC in the UK, for example, aims to inform, educate and entertain – it might be tempting to think that Netflix operates without any such limitations or restrictions.

“We have a very audacious vision, which is to entertain the world,” Larry boldly told The Big Question.

And although that is Netflix’s own mission statement, Larry also discussed some of the European legislation that makes its work more challenging.

He criticised outdated regulation for discouraging risk-taking and investment, both of which the industry urgently needs to grow and to support European talent.

Larry went on to urge policymakers to introduce consistent incentives to support investment while giving creators the freedom to tell whatever stories they want.

He fears that restrictive investment obligations could force Netflix to funnel money into shows that audiences don't actually want to watch, rather than backing productions with a good chance of success. While investment in local productions is always a good thing, producing content that nobody watches is not a sustainable business model.

US tech giant Nvidia is opening a probe into its CEO, Jensen Huang, after reports that Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company's board of directors announced on Sunday.

Nvidia is one of the global leaders in the development of artificial intelligence. Its chips power many of the data centres and computing systems used to train and run AI models. Its advanced chips have also been targeted by US export restrictions to prevent China from getting the latest semiconductor technology.

In a letter addressed to Nvidia employees, Huang said that he took "full responsibility" for his actions, while admitting to being unfaithful to his wife and apologising to his family and colleagues. However, he did not mention the name of the person involved or her reported ties to Beijing.

“Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life,” the 63-year-old wrote. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility.”

'No reason to believe' that national security has been compromised

The board leading the company, which is one of the most valuable in the world, says it has "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised, but that a thorough investigation would be carried out. The board added that Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it."

In his letter to employees, Jensen Huang said, “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security.”

Last month, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies had discovered that Huang had developed close ties with Chinese citizen and chip buyer Alice Huang, and that she was directly sharing information with Beijing.

Alice Huang is a top executive at Megaspeed, a company that runs a Singapore-based data centre and has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump was asked on Sunday whether he should have acted on the spying information sooner. However, Trump praised Huang, saying, “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. He’s done an amazing job for our country.”
